laws.rule: Utah's drink-driving limit is a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.05, lower than the 0.08 used elsewhere in the US; it took effect on 30 December 2018 (House Bill 155). A driver below 0.05 can still be charged if impaired by alcohol or drugs, including prescription medicines.
laws.penalty_signal: First-offence fines and fees can reach US$10,000 (about A$14,205 at RBA 30 Oct 2026, A$1 = USD 0.7040), with possible jail and licence suspension.

laws.rule: Having an open container of alcohol, or drinking, in the passenger area of a motor vehicle is not allowed. Alcohol may not be brought into a business open to the public, such as a grocery store, to drink there.

While a vehicle is moving, drivers may not use a phone or other device by hand to write, send or read texts, messages or email, dial a number, use the internet, take photos or video, enter data, or view videos or photos (Utah Code 41-6a-1716). Voice calls, viewing navigation, hands-free or voice use, and built-in vehicle systems are allowed.
laws.penalty_signal: First offence: class C misdemeanour, fine up to US$100 (about A$142 at RBA 30 Oct 2026, A$1 = USD 0.7040); class B misdemeanour for a repeat within 3 years or for causing serious injury.

laws.rule: Anyone launching a boat or other watercraft in Utah, including kayaks and paddle boards, must take the free annual mussel-aware boater course (about quagga mussels, a pest carried on boats). Nonresidents then pay an aquatic invasive species fee for each watercraft and get a current-year decal for the boat. Every watercraft leaving Lake Powell needs an exit inspection, then professional decontamination or a set drying time (7 days in summer, 18 in spring and autumn, 30 in winter; always 30 for wakeboard boats unless decontaminated) before launching anywhere else.
laws.penalty_signal: Nonresident fee: US$25 per watercraft (about A$36 at RBA 30 Oct 2026, A$1 = USD 0.7040).

items.text: Grocery and convenience stores may sell beer only up to 5% alcohol by volume. Liquor, wine and stronger beer to take away are sold only in state liquor stores and smaller package agencies run under the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Services; state stores generally open Monday to Saturday, from about 11 am to 7 pm or 10 pm. The drinking and buying age is 21.

In restaurants, alcohol is served only with a food order, and a restaurant must earn at least 70% of its takings from food. Full-service restaurants may serve liquor, wine and heavy beer from 11:30 am to midnight (10:30 am on weekends and holidays), and beer until 1 am. Bars must have food available but have no set food-sales share; taverns have no food requirement.

Utah allows medical cannabis only. A visitor who holds a medical cannabis card from their home state for one of Utah's qualifying conditions can apply for a non-Utah resident card, which lasts 21 days; no more than two are issued per calendar year. Cardholders show the card and ID at each pharmacy visit and meet a medical cannabis pharmacist before the first purchase.

Senate Bill 266 (2024, Medical Amendments) lets certain large Utah healthcare systems run pilot treatment programs using psilocybin or MDMA that is in late-stage (Phase 3) US Food and Drug Administration trials, only under the system's direct supervision and not for anyone under 18. Participating systems were to report results to a legislative committee before 1 July 2026. The law does not cover possession outside such a program.
The same 2024 law (Senate Bill 266) covers MDMA alongside psilocybin, for supervised pilot treatment in qualifying healthcare systems only.
